intro: This is the third movement, Allegro molto vivace, of Tchaikovsky’s Symphony No. 6 in B minor, Op. 74 “Pathétique”. Over fast string figures, a march begins as a clarinet tune played quietly and builds to a G-major ending with bass drum and cymbals. The symphony’s slow final movement follows it.

sections.label: A · Racing strings, quick woodwinds
sections.mNote: Strings run in groups of three beneath wind replies

sections.label: B · March in E major, clarinets
sections.mNote: The clarinets play the first complete statement of the march.

sections.label: A′ · The opening strings return
sections.mNote: The opening scherzo resumes after the march.

sections.label: Link · Held D before the march
sections.mNote: A held D prepares the march’s return in G

sections.label: B′ · March in G major, bass drum, cymbals
sections.mNote: The march returns with bass drum and cymbals.

sections.label: Coda · Scales falling to G major
sections.mNote: Strings and low brass descend to the final G-major chords

cues.title: Opening, strings and woodwind
cues.text: The strings play rapid groups of three, and the woodwind reply above them. Fragments of a march tune appear among the running notes. Later in the movement the full orchestra takes up this tune.
cues.evidence: Queensland Symphony Orchestra, Symphony No. 6 learning resource, p. 15: opening strings, winds and emerging march fragments. https://qso.com.au/uploads/QSO-Learning-Resource-Breathtaking-Tchaikovsky-1-.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: March theme, clarinets
cues.text: The clarinets play the march theme in full, quietly and in E major. The strings keep moving underneath.
cues.evidence: Queensland Symphony Orchestra, Symphony No. 6 learning resource, p. 15, reproduces the clarinet theme. E-major key and quiet unison scoring: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._6_(Tchaikovsky).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Corrections after the première
cues.text: On the title page of his full score Tchaikovsky added a note, apparently after the first performance: “I made some corrections in the 2nd and 3rd movements, which need to go into the parts!!! Ask Mr Kleinecke to attend to this.”
cues.evidence: Tchaikovsky’s note on the title page of the autograph score, added, it seems, after the première, as printed in the Tchaikovsky Research entry on Symphony No. 6 (Autographs). https://en.tchaikovsky-research.net/pages/Symphony_No._6

cues.title: Return of the opening scherzo
cues.text: The opening scherzo material returns. Running figures in the strings alternate with scales in the woodwind, now following the full statement of the march.
cues.evidence: Third-movement recapitulation described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._6_(Tchaikovsky); Queensland Symphony Orchestra, Symphony No. 6 learning resource, p. 15.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Dominant pedal before the march
cues.text: The preparation rests on a pedal on D, the dominant of G major. The orchestra plays over the held note before the march returns in the movement’s home key.
cues.evidence: Tchaikovsky’s third-movement sketch specifies a reprise of the scherzo with a pedal on D before the G-major march. Quoted in the composition history: https://en.tchaikovsky-research.net/pages/Symphony_No._6.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the march, G major
cues.text: The march returns in G major, now with bass drum and cymbals. The tune, first played softly by the clarinets, is taken up by the full orchestra.
cues.evidence: Third-movement G-major march and percussion scoring: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._6_(Tchaikovsky); Queensland Symphony Orchestra, Symphony No. 6 learning resource, p. 15.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Sketch inscription, February 1893
cues.text: In his February 1893 sketches, Tchaikovsky noted that his first job after returning from a trip was to compose this ending. He wanted the G-major march “in a solemnly triumphant manner”.
cues.evidence: Tchaikovsky’s inscription in the third-movement sketches, 11 February 1893 Old Style (23 February New Style), quoted at https://en.tchaikovsky-research.net/pages/Symphony_No._6.

cues.title: Reception of the march
cues.text: Critics and audiences have found this march confusing. David Brown read it as “a desperate bid for happiness so prolonged and vehement” that it confirms both the desperation of the search and its futility. The movement ends in G major, and the close often draws applause before the symphony is over.
cues.evidence: Harlow Robinson’s Boston Symphony programme note on the symphony, which quotes David Brown on the third movement and describes the G-major landing and the cheers it provokes. https://www.bso.org/works/tchaikovsky-symphony-no-6

cues.title: Closing scales in G major
cues.text: At the end of the movement, scales descend through four octaves, first in the violins and then in the low brass. The movement ends in G major. The Adagio lamentoso follows as the final movement.
cues.evidence: Harlow Robinson’s Boston Symphony programme note describes the four-octave descent and G-major landing. https://www.bso.org/works/tchaikovsky-symphony-no-6
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Clarinets complete the march tune
transitions.to: B · March in E major, clarinets
transitions.how: Fragments of the march collect into a complete E-major tune for unison clarinets. Beneath its longer notes the strings continue their running accompaniment.
transitions.evidence: Queensland Symphony Orchestra, Symphony No. 6 learning resource, p. 15; E-major clarinet scoring: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._6_(Tchaikovsky).

transitions.title: Two-bar link back to the scherzo
transitions.from: B · March in E major, clarinets
transitions.how: A two-bar link leads from the march back to the opening scherzo material. The strings return to their quick groups of three, and short wind figures cut across them. The return follows at once. The movement has no separate development section.
transitions.evidence: Third-movement exposition-to-recapitulation link: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._6_(Tchaikovsky). Queensland Symphony Orchestra, Symphony No. 6 learning resource, p. 15, describes the returning scherzo.

transitions.title: Pedal on D before the march
transitions.to: Link · Held D before the march
transitions.how: The returning scherzo reaches a pedal on D. The bass holds this dominant beneath the continuing figures and prepares G major, the key of the march’s final statement.
transitions.evidence: The composer’s third-movement sketch explicitly links the scherzo reprise, a pedal on D and the final G-major march. https://en.tchaikovsky-research.net/pages/Symphony_No._6

transitions.title: From the D pedal to the G-major march
transitions.from: Link · Held D before the march
transitions.to: B′ · March in G major, bass drum, cymbals
transitions.how: The D pedal leads to the march in G major. Strings and winds broaden the tune, and bass drum and cymbals join as the march returns. The clarinet first stated the march quietly. Here the full orchestra plays it.
transitions.evidence: Pedal and G-major destination: https://en.tchaikovsky-research.net/pages/Symphony_No._6. The final march’s scoring is described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._6_(Tchaikovsky).

transitions.title: Descending scales into the final chords
transitions.from: B′ · March in G major, bass drum, cymbals
transitions.to: Coda · Scales falling to G major
transitions.how: In the closing phrases of the march, descending scales pass through the violins and then to the trombones and tuba. The scales cover four octaves and end on G major. Brass and percussion reinforce the final chords.
transitions.evidence: Harlow Robinson, Boston Symphony programme note on Symphony No. 6, third-movement ending. https://www.bso.org/works/tchaikovsky-symphony-no-6

source.title: Tchaikovsky, Symphony No. 6, III, historical full-score scan
source.locator: PDF p. 1 running strings; march and return across the movement; final pages show full orchestral cadence. Entries describe passage-level roles, not continuous instrumentation.

timeline.note: Opening: fast violin figures, answered by the wind; the lower strings play the bass.
Early orchestral build: piccolo, brass and timpani join the running strings (score PDF pp. 12–13). The boundary given in the report at 1:22 marks the broad, louder passage before the lighter march.
First march section: a more clearly defined melody enters over continuing quick figuration in the orchestra.
First-march expansion: trumpet and bass-trombone phrases reinforce winds, horns and strings (score PDF p. 20). The report’s change at 2:38 gives an approximate anchor for the passage.
The first-march close adds piccolo to the upper winds, with trumpet punctuation (score PDF p. 22), then reduces into the scherzo return. The 3:40 report boundary anchors the region.
Scherzo return: quick string figures and wind exchanges bring back the opening texture.
Preparation: a reduced orchestral texture builds through repeated figures over a sustained foundation.
Later march section: strings, woodwind and brass enter in turn, and the percussion reinforces the louder statements.
Brass, percussion and strings reinforce the closing bars in G major.

composer.epithet: Composer who could write a brilliant ballroom scene and, within it, a single melody showing that someone present was unhappy.
facts: School of Jurisprudence; Saint Petersburg Conservatory, 1862–65, with Anton Rubinstein and Nikolai Zaremba
Nadezhda von Meck: an allowance, 1877–90, and a friendship conducted by letter
Three ballets; Eugene Onegin, The Queen of Spades and other operas
composer.background:
At Kamenka on 6 July 1878, Tchaikovsky was explaining to Nadezhda von Meck how he composed. Ideas came to him in the middle of conversations, and he kept them in his head until he could sketch them on the first sheet of paper to hand. He held that waiting for the right mood was no way to work. “Inspiration is a guest who does not like to visit the idle,” he told her. He then stopped for dinner. At two o’clock he resumed, and went on to sketching, orchestration, fair copies and how far a symphony must keep to its traditional form.

He was born in Votkinsk, where his father managed an ironworks. He grew deeply attached to his French governess, Fanny Dürbach, and began piano lessons at the end of 1845. The profession chosen for him was the law. In 1850 he entered the preparatory class of the Imperial School of Jurisprudence in Saint Petersburg. Four years later his mother died of cholera. He graduated in 1859 and took a post at the Ministry of Justice, while giving more and more of his time to opera and concerts.
